title: Vegetarian or vegan
card: Which vitamins need extra attention when you skip meat, or all animal foods.
seo: Vitamins for Vegetarians and Vegans: What You Might Be Missing
intro: A well-planned vegetarian diet can cover nearly all your vitamin needs. A few need extra attention, especially if you're vegan.
key: The big one. B12 is naturally found only in animal foods. Vegans need fortified foods or a supplement. Vegetarians who eat dairy and eggs may still run low.
D
Very few plant foods have vitamin D. Look for fortified plant milks, UV-exposed mushrooms and sensible sunshine.
B2
If you skip dairy, you lose a main source. Fortified plant milks, almonds and mushrooms help.
B9
Easy win! Dals, beans and leafy greens are packed with folate.
A
No problem. Your body makes vitamin A from carrots, pumpkin and greens. Add a little oil or ghee to absorb it.
Fe
Plant iron is absorbed less, so vegetarians need 1.8 times as much. Pair dals with vitamin C.
Zn
Zinc from beans and grains is absorbed less. Soaking and sprouting help.
O3
Flaxseed, chia or walnuts easily cover the plant omega-3 (ALA) you need.
plateTitle: A day that covers the tricky ones
plate: Fortified cereal or oats with milk or fortified plant milk
Dal, palak sabzi, roti and a bowl of curd
A handful of almonds and an orange or guava
Chana masala, brown rice and a salad with lemon squeezed on top
beyond: Beyond vitamins, vegetarians should also watch iron, zinc, calcium, iodine and omega-3 fats. We'll cover these in upcoming mineral guides.
doctor: Ask for a B12 blood test, especially if you've been vegetarian or vegan for years.
Ask about vitamin D if you get little sun.
If you're planning a pregnancy, discuss B12 and folic acid early.
protein: Vegetarians can easily get enough protein with a little planning. Build each meal around dal, beans, soy, paneer, curd or milk, and mix sources across the day.

title: Your 20s to 40s
card: Indoor jobs, takeout, weekend drinks and trendy supplements: what to watch.
seo: Vitamins in Your 20s, 30s and 40s: What Busy Adults Should Watch
intro: These are often your healthiest years. But long indoor days, skipped meals, takeout, weekend drinks and trendy supplements can quietly leave gaps, or push you over safe limits.
key: D
Office jobs, commuting and screens mean little daylight on your skin. Low vitamin D is common, even in sunny places.
B9
Anyone who could become pregnant should take 400 mcg of folic acid daily, even if not planning, because the spine forms in the first weeks.
Going plant-based? Plan your B12 from day one with fortified foods or a supplement.
B1
Regular heavy drinking, including weekend binges, drains B1 and folate.
B7
Hair, skin and nail gummies often pack huge biotin doses that can throw off blood tests.
B6
Energy drinks and pre-workouts often contain B6. Add it up across products, since long-term high doses can harm nerves.
plate: Fortified cereal or oats with milk, plus a piece of fruit
A dal, bean or chickpea bowl with greens
Almonds, sunflower seeds or a banana
Add a veggie side and squeeze lemon on top
A short walk outside at lunch
beyond: Iron (especially for women who have periods) and calcium matter in these years too. Mineral guides are coming soon.
doctor: At your yearly checkup, ask whether a vitamin D or B12 test makes sense for you.
Mention every supplement, including gummies, energy drinks and pre-workouts.
Planning a pregnancy in the next year? Start folic acid now and talk to your doctor.

title: Over 50
card: Your body absorbs some vitamins differently with age. Here's what changes.
seo: Vitamins After 50: B12, Vitamin D and What Changes With Age
intro: After 50, your body absorbs and makes some vitamins less efficiently, and many common medicines affect vitamin levels. A few small changes go a long way.
key: Less stomach acid means less B12 absorbed from food. Experts advise adults over 50 to get most of their B12 from fortified foods or a supplement.
D
Skin makes less vitamin D with age, and after 70 your daily need rises to 800 IU.
B6
Needs rise slightly after 50: 1.7 mg for men and 1.5 mg for women.
K
Important for blood clotting and bones. If you take warfarin, keep your intake steady.
Ca
Women need 1,200 mg a day from 51, and everyone from 71.
plate: A fortified cereal or fortified plant milk for B12 and D
Leafy greens for folate and vitamin K
Fatty fish or eggs, if you eat them
Some time outdoors, when it's safe
beyond: Calcium also matters more after 50 for bone health. A mineral guide is coming soon.
doctor: Bring a list of every medicine and supplement to your next checkup. Metformin and acid reducers can lower B12.
Ask whether a B12 or vitamin D test makes sense for you.
Before starting any supplement, check for interactions with your medicines.
protein: Muscle naturally shrinks with age. Expert groups suggest adults over 65 aim for 1.0–1.2 g of protein per kg a day, spread across meals, alongside strength exercise.

title: Pregnant or planning
card: Folic acid, B12, vitamin D, and what to avoid before and during pregnancy.
seo: Vitamins Before and During Pregnancy: Folic Acid, B12, D and What to Avoid
intro: Some vitamins matter even before you know you're pregnant. Here's what the evidence says. Your doctor or midwife will tailor it to you.
key: B9
Take 400 mcg of folic acid every day, starting at least a month before pregnancy. It helps prevent serious birth defects of the brain and spine. Needs rise to 600 mcg in pregnancy.
Needs rise to 2.6 mcg. Vegetarians and vegans should make sure they're covered, since low B12 affects baby's development.
D
600 IU a day. Many people start pregnancy low, so ask about testing.
A
You need some, but avoid high-dose retinol supplements and large amounts of liver, which can cause birth defects. Beta-carotene from vegetables is safe.
C
Needs rise a little, to 85 mg. Easy with fruit and veg.
Fe
Needs rise to 27 mg a day. Your doctor will check for anemia.
I
Needs rise to 220 mcg. Choose a prenatal with 150 mcg of iodine.
plate: Start a folic acid supplement (or a prenatal vitamin that has it)
Leafy greens, dals and beans for natural folate
Make sure you're not doubling up vitamin A from several supplements
Ask your doctor before trying B6 or ginger
beyond: Prenatal vitamins also contain iron, iodine and sometimes choline and DHA. All of these matter in pregnancy.
doctor: Choose a prenatal vitamin together with your doctor.
Mention any other supplements so you don't exceed safe limits.
If you're vegetarian or vegan, ask about B12 testing.
protein: Protein needs rise in pregnancy, to about 71 g a day in US guidance. Dal, eggs, dairy, fish low in mercury, soy and nuts all help.

title: Active & working out
card: Gym, running or sports: which vitamins matter, and why megadoses can backfire.
seo: Vitamins for Active Adults and Gym-Goers: What Matters and What to Skip
intro: Exercise doesn't dramatically raise your vitamin needs. Eating enough to fuel your training usually covers them. But a few vitamins deserve attention, and some popular supplements can work against you.
key: D
Supports muscles and bones. Indoor training and winter months make low levels more likely.
B2
B vitamins help turn food into energy. Vegetarian athletes may need a little more riboflavin.
Plant-based athletes should plan for B12, since low levels cause fatigue.
C
Food first. Some research suggests that high-dose vitamin C pills (around 1,000 mg a day) may blunt training gains.
E
Same story: high-dose antioxidant pills may get in the way of your body's training response. Nuts and seeds are fine.
plate: A banana or toast: easy carbs, plus some B6
Curd, milk, eggs or a chickpea bowl for protein and B vitamins
Colorful fruit and veg for vitamin C. No megadose needed
Pre-workouts often contain B6 and B12. Count them toward your total
beyond: Iron, calcium and fluids matter a lot for active people too. Women who train hard are especially prone to low iron, so ask your doctor about a ferritin test if you're often tired.
doctor: If you train hard and feel unusually tired, ask about vitamin D, B12 and iron tests.
Supplements can contain undeclared ingredients. Competitive athletes should look for third-party tested products, like NSF Certified for Sport.
Talk to a sports dietitian before taking high-dose antioxidants.
extraSource: Australian Institute of Sport: Vitamin C fact sheet
protein: Regular hard training raises protein needs to about 1.2–1.6 g per kg a day. Spread it over 3–5 meals and snacks of roughly 15–30 g each. Food works as well as powders.

title: Thinking about supplements
card: Who actually benefits, how to choose a good one, and red flags to avoid.
seo: Should I Take a Vitamin Supplement? Who Benefits and How to Choose
intro: Food first. Most people get enough of most vitamins from a varied diet. But some people really do benefit from a supplement, and some supplements can cause harm.
key: Vegans, many vegetarians, adults over 50, and people on long-term metformin or acid reducers.
B9
Anyone who could become pregnant: 400 mcg of folic acid daily.
D
People with little sun, darker skin, or older age.
plateTitle: How to choose a good supplement
plate: USP Verified, NSF Certified or ConsumerLab means the label matches what's inside
More than 100% of the daily value is rarely needed unless your doctor says so
Count vitamins across every product you take, including 'energy', 'hair' or 'immunity' blends
And your pharmacist, especially if you take any medicines
beyond: Red flags: any product that claims to 'cure', 'detox' or 'boost immunity overnight', or that warns you not to tell your doctor. Real vitamins don't need hype.
doctor: Ask whether a blood test would help before starting B12 or vitamin D.
Ask your pharmacist to check for interactions with your medicines.
Bring your supplement bottles to checkups.

title: Always tired?
card: When low vitamins might be a cause, and what to ask your doctor.
seo: Always Tired? Vitamins That Can Cause Fatigue and What to Ask Your Doctor
intro: Feeling tired all the time has many possible causes, including sleep, stress, thyroid problems, anemia, depression, diabetes and medications. Low vitamins are only one of them, but they're easy to check.
key: Low B12 can cause tiredness, weakness, tingling and memory problems. It's common in vegetarians and adults over 50.
B9
Low folate can cause a type of anemia that makes you tired and short of breath.
D
Low vitamin D is linked with tiredness and muscle aches in some people.
Fe
Low iron is a common, fixable cause of tiredness, especially with heavy periods or a vegetarian diet.
plateTitle: What to ask your doctor about
plate: Ferritin and TSH are common non-vitamin causes
beyond: Please don't self-treat with high-dose 'energy' supplements. Too much B6 can damage nerves, and supplements can hide the real cause.
doctor: See a doctor if tiredness lasts more than a few weeks or comes with weight loss, breathlessness, low mood or other symptoms.
Get urgent help for chest pain, fainting or severe breathlessness.
